t.4.23.1: Then Tārā, smelling the face of the king of monkeys, her husband, who had fallen from the world and lay dead, spoke these words.
t.4.23.3: Surely, O lord of the monkeys, the earth is dearer to you than I am, for you lie embracing her and do not answer me.
t.4.23.2: Because you did not heed my words, O hero, you now lie in pain upon the rough and cruel surface of the earth, strewn with stones.
t.4.23.4: Sugrīva indeed is valiant, O hero fond of rash deeds; yet the chiefs of the bears and monkeys wait upon you, the mighty one.
t.4.23.5: Having heard the grievous lament of these grieving ones and of Aṅgada, and this speech of mine as well, why do you not awaken?
t.4.23.6: This is that bed of heroes on which you now lie, slain in battle, the very bed on which, in former days, your enemies were laid low, struck down by you alone.
t.4.23.7: O you of pure nature and noble lineage, lover of battle, my beloved, O giver of honor, you have gone, abandoning me, helpless and alone.
t.4.23.8: Truly, a wise man should not give his daughter in marriage to a hero. Behold me, the wife of a hero, struck down and made a widow in an instant.
t.4.23.10: Surely this heart of mine is hard, made of iron, since, having seen my husband slain, it has not today burst into a hundred pieces.
t.4.23.9: My pride is shattered, and my lasting refuge is broken; I am sunk in the fathomless, vast ocean of grief.
t.4.23.11: He was indeed my friend and my husband, and dear to me by his very nature; that hero, valiant in battle, has gone to his death.
t.4.23.12: A woman bereft of her husband, even though she may indeed have sons and be amply filled with wealth and grain, is called a widow by the wise.
t.4.23.13: O hero, you lie in this pool of blood springing from your own limbs, just as if you were lying on a bed spread with a crimson coverlet.
t.4.23.14: O bull among monkeys, I cannot clasp in my arms your body, covered all over with dust and blood.
t.4.23.15: Today Sugrīva has accomplished his aim in this most terrible feud, he whose fear has been taken away by a single arrow released by Rāma.
t.4.23.17: Then Nīla drew out the arrow lodged in his body, as one might pull out a blazing venomous serpent hidden in a mountain cave.
t.4.23.16: Because of the arrow lodged in your heart, I am kept from touching your body; I can only gaze upon you, now that you have passed into death.
t.4.23.18: And as that arrow was being drawn out, its radiance shone like a ray from the sun caught upon the summit of the Western Mountain.
t.4.23.19: Streams of blood flowed from his wounds on every side, like streams mingled with copper-red ochre pouring down from a mountain.
t.4.23.20: Wiping her husband, who lay covered with the dust of battle, she bathed that hero, struck down by the weapon, with tears born of her eyes.
t.4.23.21: Seeing her husband struck down, all his limbs drenched in blood, the woman Tārā spoke to her tawny-eyed son Aṅgada.
t.4.23.22: Behold, O son, the final and most dreadful state of your father; through evil deeds, the end of this long-clinging enmity has come.
t.4.23.23: O son, salute the king, your father, the bestower of honour, whose body glows like the newly rising sun, as he departs for the abode of Yama.
t.4.23.24: Thus addressed, Aṅgada rose up and, with his two stout and rounded arms, clasped the feet of his father, saying, "I am Aṅgada."
t.4.23.25: Why do you not speak to Aṅgada as you did before, when he bows in greeting to you, saying, “Be long-lived, my son”?
t.4.23.26: With only my son for company, I sit beside you, now lifeless, like a cow with her calf sitting beside a bull just slain by a lion.
t.4.23.27: Having performed the sacrifice of battle, how is it that you have bathed in this final ablution, with the many kinds of weapons for its water, without me, your wife?
t.4.23.28: Why do I not see here on you that golden garland which the king of the gods, pleased with you in battle, once gave you?
t.4.23.29: Royal splendor does not forsake you, O giver of honor, even though your life has departed, just as the radiance of the circling sun does not forsake the king of mountains.
t.4.23.30: You did not follow this beneficial advice of mine, nor was I able to hold you back. With you slain in battle, I and my son are slain as well, and here fortune forsakes me together with you.
